title: Black-Box Red Teaming of Agentic AI: A Taxonomy-Driven Framework for Automated Risk Discovery
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence
  [Submitted on 9 Sep 2026]
    Title:Black-Box Red Teaming of Agentic AI: A Taxonomy-Driven Framework for Automated Risk Discovery
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Agentic systems are rapidly moving to production, where they read untrusted inputs, call tools with real permissions, and act autonomously, expanding the security surface beyond chat-only models. Yet standard evaluations remain single-turn and fail to capture multi-step agent vulnerabilities. We present a systematic black-box framework for risk-aware agent evaluation requiring only basic system descriptions. Our approach introduces: (1) a seven-domain taxonomy mapping observable behaviors to risk categories, (2) fully automated SAGE-RT red teaming producing 120 adversarial scenarios per domain, and (3) human-validated evaluation using LLM judges. Empirical validation across two agent architectures (CrewAI and AutoGen) with four base models reveals alarming patterns: 56.25\% average governance risk, 65\% privacy risk in multi-agent configurations, and agent behavior vulnerabilities reaching 85\%. Our black-box approach effectively identifies critical architectural vulnerabilities without privileged access, providing a scalable path toward safer agent deployments.

report.summary: A new black-box framework automatically red-teams agentic AI, uncovering governance, privacy, and behavioral vulnerabilities across CrewAI and AutoGen deployments.
report.background: Agentic AI systems are moving rapidly from demos into production, where they read untrusted inputs, call external tools with real permissions, retain memory, and act autonomously. That shift expands the security surface far beyond chat-only models: a single prompt injection or misconfigured tool can trigger multi-step failures involving data exfiltration, unauthorized actions, or inter-agent collusion. Standard safety evaluations, however, remain largely single-turn and model-centric, so they miss risks that emerge across planning, tool use, memory, and multi-agent coordination. Existing red-teaming methods are often manual, white-box, or tailored to one architecture, limiting scalability and comparability. This paper addresses that gap with a systematic black-box framework that requires only basic system descriptions, aiming to make risk discovery repeatable across diverse agent deployments.
key_points: The framework introduces a seven-domain taxonomy that maps observable agent behaviors to concrete risk categories, giving teams a shared vocabulary for governance, privacy, security, and behavioral failure modes. This structured lens helps move agent evaluation beyond ad hoc prompts toward repeatable, coverage-oriented testing.

SAGE-RT automates red teaming by generating 120 adversarial scenarios per risk domain. It operates black-box, needing only basic system descriptions rather than model weights, logs, or privileged access. That makes the method practical for third-party auditors and teams testing proprietary or hosted agents.

Evaluation combines automated scenario generation with human-validated LLM judges, balancing scale and reliability. Judges score agent responses against taxonomy-aligned criteria, while human validation helps catch false positives and judge bias, a key concern when using models to assess other models.

Testing across CrewAI and AutoGen with four base models found alarming vulnerabilities: 56.25% average governance risk, 65% privacy risk in multi-agent configurations, and agent behavior vulnerabilities reaching 85%. These results suggest failures are architectural and systemic, not limited to one model or framework.

The black-box design identifies critical architectural vulnerabilities without privileged access, offering a scalable path to safer deployments. Findings highlight that multi-agent setups can amplify privacy and coordination risks, so security reviews must cover inter-agent communication, tool permissions, and autonomy boundaries.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the paper adds pressure to treat agent security as an ongoing, automated discipline rather than a one-time model benchmark. Vendors may need to publish agent risk profiles or support third-party black-box audits, especially as regulation around AI governance and data privacy tightens. Developers should integrate multi-step red teaming into CI/CD, test tool permissions and multi-agent interactions, and assume prompt injection can succeed. Regular users may benefit from safer defaults, but they should also recognize that agents with real credentials can leak data or take unwanted actions. The framework's taxonomy and SAGE-RT pipeline could become a baseline for comparing agent safety across frameworks and models, while its high reported risk rates argue for caution before granting autonomy in sensitive workflows.
report.tools: The paper evaluates CrewAI and AutoGen, so their security documentation and sandboxing options are immediate starting points. For broader agent red teaming, explore Microsoft PyRIT, NVIDIA garak, promptfoo, and Giskard for adversarial testing, plus LLM-as-judge harnesses for scoring. Watch the arXiv page for a possible SAGE-RT code release or dataset, and follow OWASP's LLM/agent security guidance to operationalize the taxonomy.
